Course · Whole course on one page

Arithmetic and DSP on the FPGA: from the carry chain to a filter

It picks up where the buses course ends. Every widget in it runs the fn bodies of a t27 spec compiled to WebAssembly: move a slider and the spec answers.

Course 9, 27 lessons, a live widget and a t27 spec each: adders and carry chains, multipliers and the DSP48E1 slice, fixed point, CORDIC, sampling, FIR and CIC filters, the FFT, and a filter on the bench. Every number is computed by a compiled spec.

Every course is free, for everyone: no sign-up, no email, nothing to pay.

01

Module 1 · Adding numbers

Why addition is slow: the carry that walks up the word, the dedicated chain in every slice, prefix networks and carry-save trees.

01

Lesson 1 of 27

The carry chain

You will learnWhy a carry walks the whole word, and how the dedicated chain of a slice makes the walk cheap.

Bit i of a + b is the XOR of a_i, b_i and the carry into it, and the carry out is their majority. A carry made at bit 0 of 127 + 1 has to pass through bits 1 to 6 before the top bit knows its answer: the widget lights that run of 7. Recomputing the carry in a LUT costs a LUT and a route per bit; the dedicated chain of a 7-series slice costs one LUT and one route, then one hop per bit, in CARRY4 blocks of 4 bits. The spec adders.t27 states both models and leaves the three delays to you.

Try it

Load 127 + 1 and find the longest carry run; then switch to 85 + 170 and explain why the run is 0. Set the hop to 30 ps and compare the two delays for 32 bits.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Lesson 2 of 27

Looking ahead: prefix adders

You will learnHow a prefix network computes every carry in log2 n levels, and what Kogge-Stone, Sklansky and Brent-Kung pay for it.

The carries of an adder are prefixes of one associative operator, so they can be computed as a tree instead of a chain. The widget draws four networks from the spec's src() function, one dot per prefix cell. At 16 bits ripple needs 15 levels; Kogge-Stone needs 4 levels and 49 cells, Brent-Kung 7 levels and 26 cells, Sklansky 4 levels and 32 cells with a fanout of 8. The spec does not take the counts on trust: covers() replays each network on spans and checks that every column ends up covering bits 0 to i.

Try it

At 16 bits, tap bit 15 in each network and count the white dots; then name the network with the fewest levels and the one with the fewest cells.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Lesson 3 of 27

Three numbers at once

You will learnHow 3:2 counters add many numbers with almost no carry propagation, and how many layers k numbers need.

A 3:2 counter is a row of full adders with nothing between them: three numbers in, a sum word and a carry word out, and the two add up to the three. Layers of them squeeze k numbers to two before one ordinary adder finishes. The Dadda heights 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 28, 42, 63 are the most numbers each count of layers can reduce, so 9 numbers need 4 layers and 64 need 10. For 9 numbers of 16 bits that is 20 full-adder delays against 128 for a chain of adders.

Try it

Set 28 numbers and then 29: how many layers does each need, and why does one more number cost a layer? Then check that sum + carry equals a + b + c in the counter below.

Open the interactive lesson →
02

Module 2 · Multiplying

A product is a sum of shifted copies; Booth recoding halves them, and the DSP48E1 slice does the rest in one block.

04

Lesson 4 of 27

Shift and add

You will learnWhy a multiplier is a pile of shifted partial products, and how many of them a number costs.

Every 1 bit of the multiplier adds a copy of the multiplicand shifted by that bit's position; every 0 bit adds nothing. 200 x 13 is 200 + 800 + 1600 = 2600, three rows out of eight. Two 8-bit numbers make at most a 16-bit product, and an array multiplier is exactly this grid of AND gates feeding the carry-save trees of the last lesson. The spec multipliers.t27 computes each row and the running sum the widget draws.

Try it

Step through 200 x 13 row by row; then find a multiplier b from 0 to 255 that makes all eight rows add, and one that makes only one.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Lesson 5 of 27

Booth's trick

You will learnHow radix-4 Booth recoding turns eight rows into four and handles signed numbers with no special case.

Read the multiplier three bits at a time, overlapping by one, with an implicit 0 below bit 0. Each group becomes a digit from -2 to +2, and each digit one partial product: digit x a x 4^k. For 3 x 6 the digits of 6 are -2, +2, 0, 0, so the product is -6 + 24 = 18. The negative digits are what make two's complement work without a correction step. The spec checks the recoding against a x b for every pair of 8-bit numbers, all 65536 of them.

Try it

Load -128 x -128 and read the digits; then compare the Booth rows that add with the shift-and-add rows for b = 127.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Lesson 6 of 27

The DSP48E1 slice

You will learnHow a product is tiled onto 25 x 18 multipliers and how many terms the 48-bit accumulator can sum.

A DSP48E1 slice multiplies a 25-bit by an 18-bit two's complement number into a 48-bit accumulator, and the XC7A200T has 740 of them. A 25 x 18 product needs 43 bits, so the accumulator keeps 5 bits of headroom: 32 terms sum safely and the 33rd can overflow. A wider product is cut into pieces, the low ones one bit short of the port because they are unsigned: 32 x 32 takes 4 slices. The spec multipliers.t27 holds the tiling, the guard bits and the headroom.

Try it

Find the widest b that still fits one slice next to a 25-bit a; then set 16 x 16 and find the largest number of terms the accumulator holds.

Open the interactive lesson →
03

Module 3 · Fixed point

Where the binary point sits, what rounding does to a value and to its average, and what each bit of a quantizer buys.

07

Lesson 7 of 27

Q formats

You will learnHow to read and write a Qm.n fixed-point word: its range, its step and the bits around the binary point.

Qm.n has m integer bits counting the sign and n fraction bits; the word stands for its integer value times 2^-n. Q1.15 is a 16-bit word from -1 to 0.99997 in steps of 2^-15. 0.7 has no exact Q1.15 word: the nearest is 22938, worth 0.70001. The top bit weighs minus its place, which is all two's complement is. The spec fixed_point.t27 computes the range, the step, every bit and the word a value rounds to.

Try it

Store 0.7 in Q1.15 and read the error; then switch to Q2.2 and list every value the format can hold.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Lesson 8 of 27

Rounding and saturation

You will learnWhat truncation, rounding and convergent rounding do to a value and to its average, and when to wrap or saturate.

Dropping low bits is truncation, and truncation is biased: on a ramp its mean error is -0.25 LSB for one dropped bit and tends to -0.5 as more go. Round half up is biased the other way, +0.25 for one bit; convergent rounding sends ties to the even neighbour and averages to 0. Outside the range a two's complement adder wraps for free, turning 1.0 into -1.0 in Q1.15; saturation costs a comparator and keeps the sign. The spec fixed_point.t27 measures all three modes on a ramp.

Try it

Store 1.25 in Q3.1 with each rounding mode and note the stored value; then drop 4 bits and read the three biases.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Lesson 9 of 27

Quantization noise

You will learnWhy each bit of a quantizer buys about 6 dB, and where the textbook formula is optimistic.

A quantizer's error is a sawtooth one step high, and its power is the step squared over 12. Against a full-scale sine that gives 6.02 N + 1.76 dB, about 74.0 dB at 12 bits. The spec signals.t27 also measures it: it quantizes a real sine over 4096 samples holding 127 periods and divides the powers. At 12 bits the two agree; at 1 bit the formula claims 7.78 dB and the measurement finds 6.44, because so coarse an error is not uniform.

Try it

Step from 1 to 4 bits and watch the gap between the formula and the measurement close; then read what the 16th bit adds.

Open the interactive lesson →
04

Module 4 · Functions in hardware

Sine, cosine, angle and length from shifts and adds, and when a table is the better answer.

10

Lesson 10 of 27

Rotating by shifts

You will learnHow CORDIC rotation mode reaches cos and sin with nothing but shifts and adds.

Turn a vector by atan(2^-i), one way or the other, at step i: the multiply by tan is a shift by i, so each step is two shifts and two adds. Steering by the sign of the angle left drives that angle to zero, and starting at K(n) instead of 1 cancels the stretch each step adds; K(n) tends to 0.6072529350. After 16 steps, 30 degrees comes out as cos 0.866018 and sin 0.500013. The spec cordic.t27 computes every step the widget draws.

Try it

Run 30 degrees with 4 steps and then with 16, and read the errors; then find the step at which the direction first turns clockwise.

Open the interactive lesson →
11

Lesson 11 of 27

Angle and magnitude

You will learnHow CORDIC vectoring mode gives atan2 and the length of a vector without a divider.

Vectoring mode steers the other way: it turns the vector down onto the x axis and collects the angle it turned through. What is left on the x axis is the length, stretched by 1/K(n), about 1.6467602581, so one multiply by K(n) gives the magnitude. A vector in the left half-plane is first turned by 90 degrees. For (3, 4), 16 steps give a length of 5.000000 and an angle of 53.13 degrees. The spec cordic.t27 computes the steps and the references.

Try it

Drag the point into each quadrant and compare the angle with what you expect; then set 8 steps and read how far y is from 0.

Open the interactive lesson →
12

Lesson 12 of 27

Tables and interpolation

You will learnHow many sine table entries you need, and when linear interpolation beats more entries.

A quarter-wave table of n entries answers to within about half a step between them; interpolating between two entries brings that down to h^2/8, where h is pi/2 divided by n. With 16 entries of 16 bits the nearest entry is off by up to 0.049 and the interpolated answer by 0.0012. Past a point more entries buy nothing, because the b-bit words themselves are off by up to 1/(2S). The spec cordic.t27 builds the table and measures it against its own 50-step CORDIC.

Try it

Compare 16 entries with and without interpolation; then set 256 entries and find the word width at which the words, not the entries, limit the error.

Open the interactive lesson →
05

Module 5 · Signals and sampling

What sampling does to a frequency, how an oscillator is built from an adder, and what a DFT bin measures.

13

Lesson 13 of 27

Sampling and aliasing

You will learnWhy a tone above half the sample rate comes back as a lower one, and which way it folds.

A sampler sees a tone at f as one at |f - fs round(f/fs)|: the spectrum folds like paper at every multiple of fs/2. Sampled at 100, a tone at 70 is seen at 30, and so is one at 130. In every other Nyquist zone the fold runs backwards and the alias comes out mirrored. The time view shows why nothing after the sampler can tell: the samples of the 70 tone lie exactly on a 30 tone. The spec signals.t27 computes the fold, the zone and every point drawn.

Try it

Find three input frequencies that land on 30 at a rate of 100; then move fs and watch the corners of the triangle move.

Open the interactive lesson →
14

Lesson 14 of 27

A numerically controlled oscillator

You will learnHow a phase accumulator and a sine table make any frequency, and how fine the steps are.

Add a tuning word M to an N-bit accumulator every clock and its top bits sweep around a circle at f_out = M f_clk / 2^N. At 100 MHz with N = 32, M = 2^30 gives 25 MHz, a quarter turn per clock, and the next frequency up is 0.0233 Hz away. The top P bits of the phase address a sine table; the rule of thumb puts the worst phase-truncation spur about 6.02 dB per kept bit below the carrier. The spec signals.t27 picks M and computes every sample.

Try it

Ask for 1 MHz and read the tuning word and the frequency you actually get; then cut the table to 4 phase bits and look at the output samples.

Open the interactive lesson →
15

Lesson 15 of 27

Bins of a spectrum

You will learnWhat one DFT bin measures, and why a tone between bins leaks into all of them.

A DFT of L points has L bins, each fs/L wide. A tone that fits a whole number of cycles in the window lands in one bin at 0 dB and nowhere else. Move it half a bin and the peak drops to -3.7 dB and leaks into every bin, because the DFT treats the window as one period of a repeat and the repeat jumps at the seam. A Hann window tapers the seam: at 8.5 bins on 64 points it lowers bin 20 from -33.2 dB to -73.9 dB. The spec signals.t27 computes every bin.

Try it

Slide the tone from 8 to 9 bins and watch the highest bin; then switch to Hann and compare a far bin.

Open the interactive lesson →
06

Module 6 · FIR filters

The moving average, a windowed-sinc design with integer taps, and folding the taps onto DSP slices.

16

Lesson 16 of 27

The moving average

You will learnWhy averaging L samples is a low-pass filter, and where its nulls fall.

Average the last L samples and a tone at f comes out multiplied by |sin(pi f L) / (L sin(pi f))|. For L = 4 that is 1 at DC, 0.65328 at 1/8 of the sample rate and exactly 0 at 1/4: every multiple of 1/L is a null. It needs no multiplier at all, which is why FPGA designs reach for it early. The spec signals.t27 computes the response and the output sample by sample.

Try it

Put the tone on the null of L = 4 and watch the output vanish; then double L and find the new null.

Open the interactive lesson →
17

Lesson 17 of 27

Designing taps

You will learnHow a windowed-sinc low-pass is designed, and what rounding its taps to integers costs.

The ideal low-pass is a sinc; cut it to a finite number of taps and multiply by a window, and a stopband appears. With 31 taps and a cutoff of 0.1, no window leaves the stopband from 0.2 at -32.8 dB; Hamming takes it to -62.6 dB and Blackman to -76.1 dB. Then the taps become integers: at 16 bits the Hamming stopband barely moves, at 8 bits it climbs back to -32.8 dB. The spec signals.t27 designs the taps and computes both responses.

Try it

Switch between the three windows at 31 taps; then lower the coefficient bits until the bits, not the window, set the stopband.

Open the interactive lesson →
18

Lesson 18 of 27

Folding taps onto slices

You will learnHow symmetry and a fast clock cut the DSP slices a FIR needs.

A linear-phase FIR has symmetric taps, so the DSP48E1 pre-adder can add the two samples that share a tap and multiply once: 31 taps need 16 multipliers. A slice clocked C times per sample can run C of them one after another, so at 50 MHz on a 200 MHz clock 4 slices do the work, and at 48 kHz one slice does it all. The XC7A200T has 740 slices. The spec signals.t27 assigns every tap to its slice.

Try it

Compare 31 taps at 50 MHz with and without symmetry; then raise the sample rate until each slice serves one multiplier.

Open the interactive lesson →
07

Module 7 · Multirate

Lowering the sample rate without folding noise in: decimation, the CIC filter and the polyphase form.

19

Lesson 19 of 27

Lowering the rate

You will learnWhat keeping every R-th sample does to the spectrum, and which frequencies fold onto the band you keep.

Keep every R-th sample and the rate drops to fs/R, and every frequency near a multiple of the new rate lands near 0. Decimate 400 by 4 and a tone at 95 lands at 5, right inside a band of 10. The widget paints every input frequency that would fold onto the band: that is what the filter before the decimator has to remove, and why that filter can be cheap where nothing folds. The spec signals.t27 computes each fold.

Try it

With R = 4 and a band of 10, find the red zones and put a tone in each; then raise R and watch the zones multiply.

Open the interactive lesson →
20

Lesson 20 of 27

The CIC filter

You will learnHow a CIC decimator filters with no multipliers, and how many bits its registers must grow.

A CIC decimator is N integrators at the input rate, a rate change of R and N combs with delay M at the output rate. Its DC gain is (RM)^N, so its registers grow ceil(N log2(RM)) bits: with N = 4, R = 8 and M = 1 that is 4096 and 12 bits, a 16-bit input in 28-bit registers. Its response has a null at every multiple of the output rate and droops 3.6 dB at a quarter of it. The spec signals.t27 computes the gain, the growth and the response.

Try it

Set one stage and compare the response with the moving average; then load the last preset and count the register bits.

Open the interactive lesson →
21

Lesson 21 of 27

Polyphase

You will learnHow the polyphase form does the filtering of a decimator at the low rate.

Filtering at the input rate and throwing R - 1 of every R outputs away wastes R - 1 of every R multiplies. Deal the taps into R phases by k mod R instead: each phase is a short filter that only ever meets every R-th input, so all of them run at the output rate. A 31-tap decimate-by-4 filter falls from 124 MACs per output to 31. The spec signals.t27 computes the phases and the counts.

Try it

Find a tap count that splits evenly into 4 phases and one that does not; then compare the MACs at R = 8.

Open the interactive lesson →
08

Module 8 · The FFT

N log N instead of N^2: butterflies, the bit-reversed input order and the bits each stage adds.

22

Lesson 22 of 27

The butterfly

You will learnHow a radix-2 FFT breaks a DFT into stages of butterflies, and what that saves.

A butterfly takes a and b, multiplies b by a twiddle W and outputs a + Wb and a - Wb. A radix-2 FFT of N points is log2 N stages of N/2 of them: 3 stages of 4 butterflies at 8 points, 5120 butterflies at 1024 points against 1048576 multiplies for a direct DFT. The widget runs the integer FFT of the spec and shows every value: one cycle of cosine at 8 points comes out at 509 in bins 1 and 7. The spec signals.t27 computes every butterfly.

Try it

Light each stage of the 8-point FFT in turn and count the twiddles it uses; then find the stage where the value of the DC input doubles.

Open the interactive lesson →
23

Lesson 23 of 27

Twiddles and bit reversal

You will learnWhy a decimation-in-time FFT takes its input in bit-reversed order, and where the twiddles come from.

Split the input into even and odd samples, then split each half again, and the order you end up reading them in is the index with its bits reversed. At 8 points, index 1 is 001 and goes to place 4, and 3 is 011 and goes to place 6. Reversing twice gives the index back, so the reordering is a set of swaps that needs no arithmetic, only wiring. The twiddles W are points on the unit circle, cos minus j sin. The spec signals.t27 computes both.

Try it

At 16 points find every index that stays in its place; then pick an index and read its twiddle.

Open the interactive lesson →
24

Lesson 24 of 27

Growth through the stages

You will learnHow many bits the words of an FFT grow, and what halving every stage holds back and what it loses.

Every radix-2 stage can double a value, so an unscaled FFT grows up to log2 N bits, and the conservative width of the AMD FFT core is B + log2 N + 1. A full-scale DC input shows it plainly: 12 bits in, 16 bits out of a 16-point FFT, against the 17 of the rule. Halving every stage holds the word at 12 bits, but a spread signal loses a bit of precision at every stage. The spec signals.t27 runs the integer FFT the widget measures.

Try it

Run DC unscaled and halved; then run the noise input both ways and compare the largest output.

Open the interactive lesson →
09

Module 9 · On the bench

From the arithmetic to the board: a correlator from the modem spec, a budget of slices and timing, and the capstone filter.

25

Lesson 25 of 27

A correlator finds the frame

You will learnHow a Barker-13 correlator finds the start of a frame, and how many flipped chips it survives.

A frame starts with the 13 chips of the Barker code, whose correlation with itself is 13 lined up and at most 1 shifted. The modem spec bpsk.t27 pushes each received chip into a 13-chip window and correlates it; it locks at 9, well between sidelobe and peak. The widget runs those very functions on a stream of 32 chips: the peak stands at 13 where the preamble lines up, an inverted carrier gives -13, and every flipped chip in the window lowers the peak by 2.

Try it

Flip two chips of the preamble and check that it still locks; then find how many flips stop the lock.

Open the interactive lesson →
26

Lesson 26 of 27

Does it fit and close timing?

You will learnHow to budget DSP slices for a multichannel filter, and why the adder tree, not the multiplier, misses timing.

Sixteen channels of a 63-tap symmetric filter at 50 MHz on a 250 MHz clock take 7 slices each, 112 of the 740 on an XC7A200T. Whether it closes timing is a question about one register-to-register path: a direct adder tree puts ceil(log2 63) = 6 adders in it, a systolic chain through the slice cascade puts one. With the delays you set, the tree misses a 4000 ps period and the chain makes it. The spec signals.t27 counts; the timing report of your build measures.

Try it

Load the adder-tree preset, switch it to the systolic chain and read the slack; then find how many channels of the 127-tap filter fit.

Open the interactive lesson →
27

Lesson 27 of 27

Capstone: a filter on the board

You will learnHow the arithmetic of the course meets in one filter, computed bit for bit the way the board computes it.

Design the low-pass of lesson 17, feed it a passband tone and a stopband tone as 16-bit samples, and run it the way the RTL does: integer taps, a wide accumulator, round half up, saturate to 16 bits. With 31 Hamming taps of 16 bits the stopband tone is gone, the accumulator needs 32 bits, well inside the 48 of a DSP48E1, and the output stays within 1.5 LSB of the same filter in f64. To put it on the board, the chips below open the build receipt and the JTAG path.

Try it

Lower the coefficient bits to 8 and watch the error bars; then move the stopband tone into the passband and explain the output.

TRI CLAW

The agent behind t27, in Telegram and on GitHub

TRI CLAW is the project's agent: it writes and checks .t27 specs with you. Three ways to use it.

  • Free, with your own key

    Add your own API key (NVIDIA or z.ai today) and the agent runs on it. Add more keys any time.

    Add a key in Telegram ↗

  • We do it for you

    No keys to keep: join the club in our Telegram bot and the agent runs on ours. The bot shows the price before you pay.

    Join the club in Telegram ↗

  • On GitHub

    TRI CLAW is also a GitHub App, built to check the .t27 specs a pull request changes. It is not open to other repositories yet.

    Read about TRI CLAW ↗
